items.title: The History of the Witch Hat
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: When did a conical hat with a wide brim become associated with witches? The Hat Historian seems like a perfectly cromulent niche YouTube channel. Since it's October, he addresses the style of pop culture witches. Since you know witches aren't a real thing, and the many people who were executed on suspicion of being witches didn't wear such hats, it mainly comes down to a marker in art and movies to show us which one is a witch. But within that realm, there's a story to be told. Or several stories, actually, since there are various possible origins of the witch hat, which could have crossed over each other along the way.

items.title: How Knights in Shining Armor Really Fought
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Norwegian history reenactor Ola Onsrud demonstrates how 14th-century knights battled while wearing full armor, or harness, as he calls it. It's nothing like the movies. A slashing motion will get you nowhere, so it doesn't even make sense to defend yourself like the sword fights we see in film. You can see more

videos of armored hand-to-hand combat at Laughing Squid.

items.title: How They Made Casablamca
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: . I've always had a soft spot for movies that don't give us an all around happy ending. While was a near perfect film, it was chaos while filming. No one knew how it was going to end, and the script was produced day to day as they shot footage. Even when it was finished, the ending was fiddled with, and they would have kept changing it if they could. You'll learn about that and more in this video. One part that really bothered me was when they were talking about actress Madeline Lebeau and kept showing images of Ingrid Bergman in her place, but overall I learned stuff.

items.title: Tom BetGeorge"s Halloween Light Show 2026
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Tom BetGeorge has unveiled his annual Halloween light show at his home in California. It begins with his favorite movie, The Nightmare Before Christmas. The opening segment of the show "This is Halloween" uses computer synchronized music, strings of lights, lasers, drones, fire, water fountains, and projections all at once. The Jack O'Lantern in the sky is 400 feet tall, and the aerial Jack Skellington is almost as big. The second song in the show is a '90s hip hop compilation called Giant Lowrider in the Sky. 

A third segment with the song "Sabotage"by the Beastie Boys

premiers tonight at 9 Eastern.

items.title: Nikon Small World in Motion Winning Video May Be AI
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
the winners of their annual Small World in Motion competition last week. The winning video was from Dr. Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in Beijing. The video shows "abnormal beating of airway cilia from a child with Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), a genetic disorder affecting respiratory function." The above video shows the top five videos from the competition.

However, as soon as the winner was announced, other scientists started crying foul. The cilia seem to be the wrong size, and some structures seem to disappear at times. One researcher ran the video through Google Gemini and found an invisible watermark that may indicate the video was generated by artificial intelligence. Dr. Xu responded to the criticism, but since then, his comments at LinkedIn and his entire profile have been deleted. Nikon says it is re-reviewing the video and supplemental information about it. Read about

the kerfluffle in the Small World in Motion winner's seat at PetaPixel.  (via Damn Interesting)

items.title: Bus Pushes the Limits
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
We know in our heads that suspension bridges are flexible, but we don't normally see them put under so much stress that they have a visible bend. The weight limit on the one-lane Beaver Bridge in Beaver, Arkansas, is ten tons. The bus could easily be twice that, possibly several times that. You have to wonder what it feels like to ride that bus, and then you have to wonder what damage it's doing to the bridge over time. (via

Digg)

items.title: The World's Biggest Manmade Hole
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Bingham Canyon Mine in Utah is the biggest hole that humans have ever dug. Copper was discovered in the area in 1848, and they've been digging it out ever since. An open-pit mine proved to be the easiest way to extract the massive seam of low-grade porphyry copper ore, which also yields some gold, silver, lead, molybdenum, platinum, and palladium. The key to reaching it was explosives. What could possibly go wrong? 

Let's count: the danger of the explosives, the sheer work put into the project, the extra work to extract copper and other metals from the 400,000 tons of material removed every day, toxic chemicals exposed (it's a Superfund site), displaced residents, contaminated groundwater, the threat of flooding, and the danger of collapse. There's probably more, but the mine is quite profitable, even after all this time, so they'll keep digging the world's biggest hole even bigger. The video is only 5:37; the rest is an ad.
